heading: Bringing back bison, caribou and fire
intro: This lab asks how ecosystems recover after a disturbance, and who helps them recover. In the Edmonton area, across Alberta and in northeastern British Columbia, First Nations and Métis communities are leading work to bring back bison, caribou and fire, using their own knowledge alongside science. These connections name the nations doing that work and point to them as the people who hold the knowledge.

connections.title: Elk Island bison return to Indigenous communities
connections.text: Elk Island National Park, east of Edmonton, sits on the Beaver Hills plateau, known as Amiskwaciy (Beaver Hills) to Cree peoples. The park's bison herds grow quickly, so animals are moved out to keep the herds healthy. Parks Canada reports that over five years it transferred 212 bison to their traditional homelands in nine Indigenous communities. In 2022, Métis Crossing near Smoky Lake received 20 wood bison, and Beaver Lake Cree Nation received four. Seven calves were born at Métis Crossing in 2023. Its CEO, Juanita Marois, says they are "trying to re-establish the natural environment that would have been there."

sources.title: Parks Canada: Elk Island National Park Management Plan, 2023

connections.title: Banff's bison: knowledge and science together
connections.text: The 16 plains bison moved to Banff National Park in 2017 grew to over 130 animals by 2024. Parks Canada says much of the project's success comes from weaving Indigenous ceremonies and cultural knowledge with western science. Its Indigenous Advisory Circle includes the Siksika, Kainai, Piikani and Tsuut'ina Nations, the Stoney Nakoda Nations (Bearspaw, Chiniki and Goodstoney) and the Otipemisiwak Métis Government. The Stoney Nakoda Nations wrote their own cultural monitoring report and recommended that cultural monitoring fieldwork continue. In 2014, Kainai, Siksika, Piikani and Tsuut'ina were among the first eight nations to sign the Buffalo Treaty, which recognizes buffalo as "an important part of the ecological system."

sources.title: Parks Canada: Plains bison reintroduction, Banff National Park

connections.title: Communities returning fire to the land
connections.text: Some Indigenous communities in Alberta are leading the return of planned fire. Beaver Lake Cree Nation, about 215 km northeast of Edmonton, and East Prairie Métis Settlement are working with Alberta Wildfire to burn stretches of land at risk of catching fire. Shane Bair, fire chief at Beaver Lake Cree Nation, trained in traditional burning through the We Are Fire program. He says burns "rejuvenate the land, helps get the medicines back." In Waterton Lakes National Park, members of Kainai Nation have worked side by side with Parks Canada fire crews to return fire to the land. How cultural burning is done is for these communities to teach.

sources.title: CBC News: Indigenous communities turn to prescribed burns to protect land from wildfires

connections.title: Klinse-Za caribou: a herd brought back
connections.text: Near Chetwynd, in northeastern British Columbia, Saulteau First Nations and West Moberly First Nations lead the recovery of the Klinse-Za mountain caribou herd. Saulteau First Nations is a Treaty 8 Nation. In 2013, fewer than 40 caribou were left. The Nations use three tools together. Maternal penning protects pregnant females and their calves from predators. Predator numbers are reduced. Damaged habitat is restored. Saulteau First Nations reports the herd passed 140 animals in 2024. A 2020 partnership also helped create a much larger Klinse-za Park to protect caribou habitat. Naomi Owens-Beek of Saulteau First Nations says: "Indigenous conservation is real, it's happening."

sources.title: Saulteau First Nations: Treaty Rights and Environmental Protection
CBC News: Indigenous-led recovery effort triples caribou herd
CBC News: Klinse-za Park expansion near Chetwynd

try: Banff's bison herd grew from 16 in 2017 to over 130 in 2024. The Klinse-Za caribou herd grew from fewer than 40 in 2013 to over 140 in 2024. A head count is one kind of monitoring data. The Stoney Nakoda Nations also asked for cultural monitoring. What might people who know the land notice that a head count would miss?

Roads and other cleared lines through a forest are a human disturbance. Rachel Plotkin of the David Suzuki Foundation, speaking about Klinse-za Park, says these "linear disturbances increase the sightlines for predators." How do maternal penning, predator reduction and habitat restoration each deal with a different cause of the caribou decline? Which one helps the ecosystem most over the long term, and why?

Parks Canada says cultural burning enhances biodiversity and reduces wildfire risk by reducing vegetation. Use your results from the forest manager simulation to explain why planned fire can increase habitat variety. Why does it matter that the communities who hold this knowledge are the ones who teach how it is done?

slide.title: Bringing back bison, caribou and fire
points: Edmonton area: Elk Island has sent 212 bison home to nine Indigenous communities, including Métis Crossing and Beaver Lake Cree Nation.
Alberta: First Nations and the Otipemisiwak Métis Government advise Banff's bison project. The herd grew from 16 to over 130.
Canada: Saulteau and West Moberly First Nations grew the Klinse-Za caribou herd from under 40 to over 140.
slide.notes: Use with Lesson 6 (caring for ecosystems) and Lesson 7 (forest management). Ask: which intervention from the lab is each example, and what monitoring data would show it is working? Also mention that Beaver Lake Cree Nation, East Prairie Métis Settlement and Kainai Nation are returning planned fire to the land with Alberta Wildfire and Parks Canada. Do not describe how cultural burning is done; that is for those communities to teach. Point students to the Ways of knowing section in the lab for sources and discussion prompts.

review_flags: Existing lab sentence, Lesson 6 and deck slide notes ("Many First Nations have long worked to bring bison back to the land, and several Indigenous Guardian programs in Alberta now help monitor wildlife and water"): I found sources that support it and propose this sourced rewording, to be applied when you approve: "First Nations and Métis communities are bringing bison back. Elk Island National Park has sent 212 bison to nine Indigenous communities, and in 2014 Kainai, Siksika, Piikani and Tsuut'ina were among the first nations to sign the Buffalo Treaty. Indigenous Guardians also monitor the land in Alberta: Fort McKay First Nation's Guardians monitor wildlife, air and water quality, Chipewyan Prairie First Nation is building a Guardian program for woodland caribou habitat, and the Métis Nation of Alberta's Askîy Guardians report on berries, fish, wildlife and water." Sources: Parks Canada Elk Island Management Plan 2023 (https://parks.canada.ca/pn-np/ab/elkisland/info/plan/gestion-management-2023); International Buffalo Relations Institute (https://buffalorelations.land/buffalo-treaty/); ECCC, 47 First Nations Guardians initiatives 2025 to 2026 (https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/news/2025/12/47-first-nations-guardians-initiatives-20252026.html); Métis Nation of Alberta, Askîy Initiative (https://albertametis.com/programs-services/environment-climate/environment-team/askiy-initiative/). Approve, edit, or keep the original.

Existing Bench 5 card ("Species relocation", who: "Parks Canada, Elk Island and Banff national parks, First Nations partners, scientists"): would you like "First Nations partners" replaced with the named Indigenous Advisory Circle? Parks Canada lists: Siksika Nation, Stoney Nakoda Nations (Bearspaw, Chiniki and Goodstoney), Kainai Nation, Piikani Nation, Tsuut'ina Nation, and the Otipemisiwak Métis Government (Rocky View and Red Deer Métis Districts).

Cultural burning: the fire connection says only who is doing the work and where, and points to the communities as the teachers. I did not use Shane Bair's line that traditional burning "has been lost to many Indigenous communities in Alberta" to avoid deficit framing. Note that the April 2024 burn at Beaver Lake Cree Nation is described by CBC as an Alberta Wildfire prescribed burn, so I wrote "working with Alberta Wildfire" rather than saying the Nation led it. Are you comfortable including this connection, or should it wait until a community partner (for example the Beaver Lake Cree Nation fire department) can be asked?

Numbers differ across sources. Buffalo Treaty: CBC (2014) says 11 tribes signed and the date varies (September 23, 24 or 25, 2014) across sources; I used the treaty keepers' own count of eight original nations and only the year. Klinse-Za: 2013 counts are 36, 38 or "under 40"; recent counts are 114 (2022), 138 (2024, CBC) and "over 140 in 2024" (Saulteau First Nations). I used Saulteau First Nations' own figures. Please confirm.

Edmonton scale: I could not find a well-sourced fit inside the North Saskatchewan River valley itself, so this connection uses Elk Island (Amiskwaciy, the Beaver Hills). I used Parks Canada's spelling "Amiskwaciy". Do you want it kept as Parks Canada writes it, or matched to another spelling you use? The Elk Island plan also says Parks Canada has collaborated with "the Treaty 6 First Nations in Alberta" and sets a target to establish an Indigenous Advisory Circle for Elk Island within five years; I did not find whether it exists yet, so I left it out.

Métis Crossing: CBC places it in Smoky Lake, "about 115 km north of Edmonton". I wrote only "near Smoky Lake". APTN's article reporting the 2022 transfers (20 wood bison to Métis Crossing, four to Beaver Lake Cree Nation) is undated on the fetched page.

Peoples field for Klinse-Za: Saulteau First Nations describes itself as a mixture of Dunne-Zaa (Beaver), Néhiyawak (Cree), Iyarhe Nakoda (Stoney), Haudenosaunee and Nahkawē (Saulteau) people. I did not find a West Moberly First Nations self-description, so I listed the two nations by name instead of labelling them Anishinaabe (Saulteaux). Is that acceptable?

Alberta bison connection: "Niitsitapi (Blackfoot)" in the peoples field is my grouping of Siksika, Kainai and Piikani; none of the fetched pages in this draft uses the word Niitsitapi. Please confirm or remove. I also did not mention the Indigenous Advisory Circle's ceremonial bison harvest, on purpose.

Inuit Nunangat: I did not include an Inuit connection. I did not find, in this task, an Inuit-led source that fits succession or disturbance as directly as the caribou and bison examples. If you want one, Inuit-led monitoring of changing Arctic ecosystems could be researched in a later revision.

Knowledge Keeper or Guardian visit: still open, as the lab already suggests. Beaver Lake Cree Nation, Métis Crossing and the Métis Nation of Alberta's Askîy Guardians are all named in sources here as possible contacts.
